safe_temperature.temperature: 145°F (62.8°C) or until flesh is opaque and separates easily with a fork

source.name: SAFE MINIMUM INTERNAL TEMPERATURES as measured with a food thermometer - FDA

safe_temperature.disagreements: The FDA standard specifies a minimum internal temperature of 145°F (flesh opaque and flaking easily). However, culinary sources in the notebook (Prime Women, Dishing Out Health, Harvard Nutrition Source) note that cooking wild or farmed salmon to 145°F in dry heat expels white albumin protein and can dry out delicate flakes; culinary preference frequently targets 125°F to 130°F (medium-rare to medium) before a 3-minute rest, during which carryover heat brings the fish to a tender, juicy, and buttery finish.

methods.cut: salmon fillets (skin-on or skinless, 4 to 6 oz portions) or whole side
methods.time: 15 to 20 minutes at 375°F, or 12 to 15 minutes at 400°F (standard rule: 10 minutes per inch of fillet thickness)
methods.doneness: Internal temperature reaches 145°F; flesh becomes opaque and flakes easily when tested gently with a fork
methods.rest: 3 to 5 minutes tented loosely before serving
methods.tips: Drizzle fillets with olive oil, lemon slices, and fresh dill; baking inside folded parchment paper or aluminum foil packets (en papillote) traps aromatic steam and allows salmon to absorb herb and citrus flavor without requiring added fats; when roasting on a sheet pan with baby potatoes, roast potatoes first before adding salmon for the final 12-15 minutes.

source.name: 7 Nutrient-Packed Recipes That Make Healthy Eating a Breeze - Prime Women & Food Network
source.location: Baked Salmon with Lemon and Dill & Salmon Baked in Foil

methods.heat: Medium-high heat in a heavy cast-iron or stainless steel skillet
methods.time: 4 to 5 minutes skin-side down, then 2 to 3 minutes on flesh side (approx. 7 to 8 minutes total)
methods.doneness: Skin is golden-brown, crackling, and shatter-crisp; flesh is opaque on edges and tender throughout
methods.rest: 2 to 3 minutes on a warm plate; do not cover skin with foil to preserve crackling crispness
methods.tips: Thoroughly pat salmon skin completely dry with paper towels; score skin lightly with a sharp knife; press down gently with a spatula during the first 30 seconds of searing to prevent the fillet from curling; baste flesh with foaming butter, lemon juice, and capers during the final minute off heat.

source.name: Recipes - The Nutrition Source | Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
source.location: Crispy Skin Pan-Roasted Salmon with Lemon & Capers

methods.heat: High broil setting (rack positioned 4 to 6 inches from upper heating element)
methods.time: 6 to 8 minutes total (3 minutes per side, or 6 to 7 minutes without flipping for skin-on fillets)
methods.doneness: Exterior glaze is caramelized and lightly blistered; interior is opaque and flaking tenderly
methods.tips: Line baking sheet with foil and coat lightly with cooking spray; watch closely as sweet glazes (miso, honey-mustard, teriyaki) caramelize rapidly under high broil and can scorch if left unattended.

source.name: Recipes - The Nutrition Source | Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health & Food Network
source.location: Classic Miso-Glazed Broiled Salmon & Honey-Mustard Glazed Baked Salmon

methods.heat: Medium heat to sear, then reduced to low heat gentle simmer in sauce
methods.time: 3 minutes initial sear per side, followed by 5 to 7 minutes simmering in sauce
methods.doneness: Salmon flakes tenderly with a fork and absorbs rich pan sauce aromatics
methods.rest: None; serve immediately bathed in sauce
methods.tips: Sear salmon first to develop fond, transfer temporarily to a plate, build creamy sauce (garlic, sun-dried tomatoes, artichoke hearts, spinach, broth/cream), then return salmon to finish gently in the sauce.

avoid.warning: Overcooking salmon: cooking past 145°F causes muscle fibers to contract violently, squeezing out natural oils and white coagulated albumin, leaving the fish chalky and dry.
Failing to pat skin dry before pan-searing: surface moisture generates steam in the skillet, preventing the skin from crisping and causing it to tear and stick to the pan.
Trapping steam under tight foil during resting: wrapping crispy-skin salmon tightly in foil softens the crackling crust within minutes.
Leaving high-sugar glazes unmonitored under the broiler: honey, maple syrup, and miso glazes caramelize rapidly and will scorch if placed too close to the broiler element.
